summary: Mission Control: Design a Space Mission is a browser game where players design and fly a complete space mission, solo or in online teams of up to four. Players pick a mission, then choose instruments, a spacecraft body, solar panels, a battery, a radio, an orbit, a rocket, and ground stations under a fixed budget. Every choice changes mass, power, data, communications, and cost. A design review blocks launches that break hard limits, and a simulation then plays out the mission, including rocket failures and random events. The final report explains the result in plain language. The game teaches that science only counts if its data reaches the ground.
details:
Mission Control: Design a Space Mission lets one player, or a team of up to four, design and fly a complete space mission. Players choose Wildfire Watch or Lunar Ice Hunter, then pick instruments, the spacecraft body, power, radio, orbit, rocket, and ground stations under a fixed budget. Every choice changes mass, power, data, communications, and cost. A design review blocks launches that break hard limits and warns when margins are thin. The mission then simulates launch and years of operations, including failures. A final report explains the score in plain language. The core lesson is that science only counts if it reaches the ground.

It lets students and new engineers try designs, fail safely, and see why a decision helped or hurt. The goal is to connect separate topics, such as orbits and instruments, into the trade-offs a real mission team has to make.

We built it in Godot 4.7 with GDScript and exported it for the web. Online play uses a small Node.js WebSocket relay so each player owns one role: Mission Lead, Science Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, or Operations Lead. The rules follow NASA systems-engineering ideas: set the objective first, then balance the launch, space, and ground segments, keep margins, and pass a design review. A short tutorial, tooltips, and a glossary explain terms as they appear, so players do not need prior space knowledge.

The creative part is turning those trade-offs into play. Roles want different things, spare parts and margins pay off when something breaks, and the report teaches from the player’s own numbers instead of marking answers right or wrong. We focused on beginner clarity, realistic limits, both solo and team play, and a complete mission loop that someone can finish and learn from.
